strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively underexplored setting: full-surround semantic scene completion from one panoramic camera on legged platforms, where payload constraints, projection distortion, and body motion are practically relevant.

The proposed design is reasonably coherent. Dual raw/equirectangular processing and Cartesian/cylindrical grids are well motivated by panoramic geometry, while the architecture and losses are described with useful diagrams and equations.

The reported quantitative results are promising. OneOcc improves over camera-only MonoScene from 19.19 to 20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc, from 33.46 to 37.29 on H3O within-city, and from 24.15 to 32.23 on H3O cross-city. The H3O improvements cover many semantic classes rather than only the dominant road classes.

Providing both a real quadruped dataset and a controlled synthetic human-ego dataset could be a useful contribution. The evaluation includes several vision and LiDAR baselines, per-class results, lighting-condition breakdowns, cumulative ablations, and basic runtime measurements.
weaknesses: The benchmark protocols are insufficiently documented to support the headline results. QuadOcc contains only 10 scenes from one campus and reports a validation set, but the exact sequence-level split is not given. Because the data comprise 24K consecutive frames and training uses stride 5, it is unclear whether temporally adjacent or spatially overlapping frames occur across training and validation. This could materially inflate performance. H3O likewise lacks exact sequence assignments and sufficient detail about occupancy generation and simulated gait.

The real-data ground truth procedure is not rigorous enough for a new benchmark. The paper mentions multi-frame LiDAR aggregation, Grounded-SAM initialization, and targeted manual corrections, but does not specify synchronization, pose compensation, aggregation windows, treatment of moving objects, annotation coverage, or quantitative quality control. These omissions are especially consequential because gait motion and dynamic classes are central to the claims.

The evidence does not establish that GDC provides meaningful gait compensation. It predicts only a global 2D translation per feature scale from a single globally pooled frame. Roll, pitch, and motion of a panoramic camera generally create spatially varying spherical warps rather than a uniform image-plane shift. There is no temporal input, motion supervision, evaluation versus gait magnitude, recovered-displacement analysis, or comparison with geometric pose correction. Its only evidence is a +0.39 mIoU step in one cumulative ablation without repeated-run variance.

The component attribution is incomplete and partly inconsistent. On H3O the raw-projection branch is disabled, so the claimed DP-ER module is not actually present, yet the cross-city improvement is attributed in part to DP-ER. No H3O ablation is reported. On QuadOcc, the strictly cumulative ablation cannot isolate components or their interactions, and the individual improvements of 0.26–0.41 mIoU are difficult to assess without multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility is currently poor. The manuscript omits essential details such as the encoder backbone, feature dimensions, number of experts, polar-grid construction and spatial ranges, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, training duration, exact data splits, class weights, depth predictor, and substantial baseline-adaptation details. The promised code/data URL is blank, so neither the datasets nor implementation are presently available for verification.

The claimed lightweight, deployable nature is not supported by the measurements: the model has 101.76M parameters and runs at 14.3 FPS on an RTX 4090, with no FLOP count or matched efficiency comparison to baselines. The Jetson Thor projection assumes linear scaling from peak tensor-core throughput and invokes 2:4 sparsity without demonstrating that the model uses such sparsity; it is not credible deployment evidence.

The individual methodological ingredients—dual projections, cylindrical/Cartesian representations, attention, mixture-of-experts fusion, and learned sampling offsets—are mostly established ideas. The paper does not experimentally compare against the closest cited panoramic/cylindrical occupancy approaches, making the incremental method contribution difficult to distinguish. Overall, the potentially valuable dataset direction and promising numbers are outweighed by unresolved split/annotation validity, weak support for the gait-specific claim, and inadequate reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored problem: full-surround semantic scene completion from one panoramic camera on legged or human-ego platforms.
The proposed QuadOcc and Human360Occ benchmarks could be useful contributions, covering real quadruped data, varied lighting, synthetic cross-city evaluation, and small classes relevant to robotics.
The reported improvements are promising: 20.56 versus 19.19 mIoU on QuadOcc, 37.29 versus 33.46 within-city on H3O, and 32.23 versus 24.15 cross-city. Per-class results are also provided.
The evaluation includes multiple LiDAR and vision baselines, cumulative component ablations, lighting-specific results, qualitative examples, and basic latency and memory measurements.
weaknesses: The central gait-robustness claim is inadequately tested. GDC is supported only by a +0.39 mIoU step in one cumulative QuadOcc ablation. There is no controlled jitter experiment, performance stratified by motion magnitude, displacement accuracy, or comparison with geometric stabilization. Moreover, a global 2D translation inferred from one frame cannot generally correct roll, pitch, rotation, or spatially varying panoramic warps.

Several technical definitions are incomplete or inconsistent. Equation 12 does not clearly incorporate the resampled polar volume that AMoE-3D is said to fuse. In Equation 13, the summed gradient norms appear scalar, making the subsequent 3D convolution and voxel-wise gating dimensionally unclear. Expert definitions, gate dimensions, scale-weight computation, validity masks, and out-of-view handling are insufficiently specified. The formulation also defines labels 0 through C but only C logit channels.

The H3O evidence contradicts part of the causal explanation. The implementation section says the raw-projection branch is disabled on H3O, meaning DP-ER is absent, yet the cross-city improvement is attributed to DP-ER and AMoE-3D. No H3O ablation identifies the source of the large +8.08 gain, and GDC also appears disabled or optional there.

Dataset construction and split integrity are insufficiently documented. For QuadOcc, the exact train/validation scenes, temporal separation, routes, sensor synchronization, LiDAR aggregation window, dynamic-object treatment, annotation quality control, and audit statistics are missing. Given 24K consecutive frames from only 10 scenes and a vaguely described split, near-duplicate or map leakage cannot be excluded. H3O likewise lacks exact map identities, route generation, gait simulation, and leakage controls.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty and sufficiently diagnostic controls. Results are reported from single runs without confidence intervals or variance, which is important for the small QuadOcc improvement and rare classes. The cumulative ablation does not isolate individual components or their interactions. Simpler parameter-matched alternatives such as augmentation, circular padding, conventional dual-view fusion, and a non-MoE decoder are not tested.

The lightweight and deployability claims are unsupported. OneOcc has 101.76M parameters and achieves 14.3 FPS in FP32 or 18.9 FPS with mixed precision on an RTX 4090. There are no baseline efficiency comparisons or measurements on onboard hardware. The Jetson Thor estimate improperly extrapolates runtime from theoretical tensor-core throughput, including 2:4 sparsity without demonstrating that the model uses such sparsity.

The comparison protocol is not reproducible enough to establish fairness. The paper omits backbone, optimizer, learning rate, epochs, augmentations, pretraining, expert count, and many sampling details. Baselines receive different modalities and their adaptation and tuning budgets are unclear. Surpassing older LiDAR methods on this coarse, short-range grid therefore does not substantiate a broad camera-versus-LiDAR superiority claim.

The real-data scope is narrow relative to the robotics motivation: one campus, 10 scenes, six coarse classes, and no downstream navigation, foothold, collision-avoidance, calibration-drift, or closed-loop evaluation. Claims about occlusion recovery and 360-degree continuity are supported only by a small selected qualitative panel rather than dedicated metrics.

Reproducibility is poor because the abstract contains an empty availability statement and neither dataset nor code is actually accessible from the manuscript. Since the new datasets underpin nearly all conclusions, this and the missing split and annotation specifications are material scientific weaknesses.

Overall, the problem and reported results have merit, but consequential gaps in technical specification, dataset validation, controlled evidence, and reproducibility currently outweigh the contribution, leading to a weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2bd097d97ccb4f4786a241645c02ba34/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a relevant and underexplored setting: full-surround semantic scene completion from a single panoramic camera on legged platforms, where sensor payload and field of view are important practical constraints.

The combination of a real quadruped dataset (QuadOcc: 24K frames) and a synthetic benchmark with within-city and cross-city protocols (H3O: 8K frames over 16 maps) is potentially valuable to the community and broadens evaluation beyond conventional driving datasets.

The quantitative results are consistently favorable. OneOcc obtains 20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc versus 19.19 for MonoScene and 18.44 for LMSCNet, and its larger H3O gains—37.29 versus 33.46 within-city and 32.23 versus 24.15 cross-city—support the usefulness of the overall design.

The authors compare against several representative camera- and LiDAR-based SSC systems, report per-class and geometry metrics, examine day/dusk/night conditions, and include qualitative examples. The improvements on rare H3O classes such as trucks, buses, two-wheelers, and poles are particularly encouraging.

The component study shows monotonic improvements from GDC (+0.39 mIoU), dual projection (+0.31), bi-grid voxelization (+0.41), and AMoE-3D (+0.26). Although small individually, the gains are distributed across multiple classes rather than arising solely from a dominant class.

The paper is generally well organized, and the motivation connecting panoramic geometry to dual projections and cylindrical voxelization is intuitive. The method is technically plausible and relevant to computer vision and embodied perception.
weaknesses: Material: The evidence specifically supporting gait robustness is limited. GDC predicts only a global 2D translation from single-frame features, whereas gait-induced roll, pitch, blur, rolling-shutter distortion, and spatially varying equirectangular motion generally cannot be corrected by a uniform shift. The paper provides no controlled evaluation by gait phase or motion magnitude, no comparison against generic learned/deformable alignment, and no analysis of the predicted displacements. Thus, the +0.39 mIoU gain establishes that the module helps, but not that it compensates gait displacement as claimed.

Material: Dataset construction and evaluation protocols are insufficiently documented for two contributions positioned as new benchmarks. QuadOcc has only 10 scenes, but exact train/validation scene counts, spatial ranges, sequence separation, per-condition sample counts, and safeguards against correlation among consecutive frames are missing. Its ground truth combines multi-frame LiDAR, Grounded-SAM, and manual fixes, yet annotation accuracy, dynamic-object handling, aggregation windows, and quality-control measurements are not reported.

Material: The ablation is cumulative and apparently based on one run. Improvements of 0.26–0.41 mIoU may be comparable to training variance, but no repeated-run statistics or isolated/factorial ablations are given. There are also no corresponding H3O ablations, even though the paper attributes the large cross-city gain to particular modules.

Material: Some interpretations exceed the experiments. The paper attributes H3O cross-city robustness partly to DP-ER, while the implementation section says that the raw-projection branch is disabled on H3O, removing the central dual-projection mechanism. Similarly, comparisons with selected LiDAR baselines on a coarse, short-range, newly introduced benchmark do not establish a general camera-versus-LiDAR advantage.

Material: The deployment claim is not convincingly demonstrated. The model has 101.76M parameters and achieves 14.3 FPS in FP32 or 18.9 FPS with mixed precision on an RTX 4090. The claimed Jetson Thor performance is only a linear extrapolation from peak tensor-core throughput, including a sparsity-qualified figure, and ignores memory bandwidth, unsupported operations, and utilization. Actual embedded-device measurements or, at minimum, FLOPs and matched efficiency comparisons are needed to substantiate the characterization as lightweight and onboard-ready.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details are absent, including encoder identity, channel widths, number of experts K, polar-grid resolution and bounds, cross-grid sampling details, optimizer, learning rate, epochs, augmentation, class weights, and baseline adaptation settings. Equation 6 also omits a view index despite sampling both projections, while the GradEnergy3D norm in Equation 13 appears scalar as written and is therefore incompatible with the stated convolutional voxel-wise gate. The promised code and datasets are not presently linked in the manuscript.

Presentation refinement: The paper should separate demonstrated findings from hypotheses more carefully—for example, explanations for LiDAR lighting trends and claims about sharper foothold decisions are not directly evaluated. These issues are correctable and do not outweigh the promising benchmark contribution and consistent empirical gains.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored setting: full-surround semantic scene completion for legged platforms using one panoramic camera. The combination of a real quadruped dataset (QuadOcc) and a controlled simulated human-ego dataset (H3O) could be useful to the community.

The empirical study is unusually broad. It retrains several camera and LiDAR baselines, reports per-class and completion metrics, evaluates within-city and cross-city generalization, stratifies QuadOcc by lighting, and includes calibration, field-of-view, resolution, temporal-fusion, and range-wise analyses.

The main results are promising: OneOcc improves over MonoScene from 19.19 to 20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc and from 33.46/24.15 to 37.29/32.23 on H3O within-/cross-city. The particularly large cross-city improvement is meaningful, and gains occur across rare H3O classes rather than only dominant road categories.

The manuscript is clear and visually polished, gives equations for the principal components, provides extensive baseline implementation details, and reports desktop and Jetson AGX Orin latency. The bi-grid ablation also supports its intended near/far complementarity: compared with Cartesian-only, Bi-Grid improves near mIoU from 36.42 to 37.35 and far mIoU from 30.56 to 32.23.
weaknesses: The central gait-compensation claim is not convincingly established. GDC predicts only a global 2D shift from a single frame; such a shift cannot generally invert depth-dependent camera translation, roll, spatially varying panoramic distortion, or within-exposure motion blur. Its measured contribution on QuadOcc is only +0.39 mIoU, without repeated-run variance, a controlled gait-intensity evaluation, or comparison to optical stabilization/augmentation alternatives. Figure 8 shows selected predicted offsets but no ground-truth displacement or quantitative correlation.

Attribution of the overall gains is incomplete. The QuadOcc ablation is cumulative rather than factorial, and each reported increment is only 0.26–0.41 mIoU. Meanwhile, OneOcc also changes the image encoder and replaces MonoScene's decoder with a depthwise architecture. H3O, where the headline cross-city gain is +8.08, lacks an end-to-end ablation against a backbone- and decoder-matched baseline, so the gain cannot be confidently assigned to BGV or AMoE-3D.

QuadOcc ground-truth semantics are initialized by applying Grounded-SAM to the same panoramic RGB modality used as model input, then transferring those labels to LiDAR and applying unspecified targeted manual corrections. This can imprint image-model errors and correlations into the evaluation labels. No quantitative annotation audit, independently labeled subset, inter-annotator agreement, or error rate is reported, which materially weakens conclusions drawn from the real benchmark.

The QuadOcc evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified despite the long supplement. The paper states that it has ten scenes, an 'official' sequence-heterogeneous train/validation split, and stride-5 training, but does not provide the scene allocation or train/validation counts. With 24K consecutive frames and temporally aggregated labels, sequence independence is essential to rule out near-duplicate or map-level leakage.

There are internal coordinate inconsistencies affecting reproducibility and potentially baseline fairness. Dataset construction repeatedly defines the vertical range as [-2.0, 1.2] m, but several baseline configurations state an origin of -1.2 m for the 8-bin, 0.4 m grid; H3O MonoScene similarly lists -2.4 m. The supplement later calls -1.2 m the ground-truth convention while also claiming a [-2.0, 1.2] m crop. These descriptions cannot all define the same aligned volume.

The novelty is primarily an integration of familiar ingredients—dual views, cylindrical/Cartesian representations, attention/MoE fusion, and learned sampling offsets. Some positioning is also overstated: the full QuadOcc dual-projection model has 189.83M parameters, 26% more than MonoScene, and the dual branch yields only +0.53 mIoU over ER-only while adding 86.5% parameters. Thus the broad 'lightweight' and camera-versus-LiDAR claims should be interpreted cautiously, especially since the LiDAR comparison uses a limited set of mostly older SSC architectures.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored setting: single-camera 360-degree semantic occupancy for legged platforms. The combination of a real quadruped dataset (QuadOcc) and a synthetic, map-disjoint benchmark (H3O) could be useful to the community.

OneOcc reports consistent improvements over the retrained camera baselines. The strongest evidence is on H3O-Heter, where it improves mIoU from 24.15 for MonoScene to 32.23, with gains across all reported classes. The paper also evaluates lighting, calibration perturbations, field of view, temporal aggregation, resolution, and embedded runtime.

The supplement provides extensive implementation and dataset-construction details. It includes per-class results, baseline adaptation descriptions, parameter breakdowns, and measured Jetson AGX Orin latency rather than relying solely on theoretical complexity.

The bi-grid study provides some empirical support for combining Cartesian and cylindrical representations: on H3O-Heter, Bi-Grid improves overall IoU from 45.84/47.57 for the two single-grid variants to 49.58. The cross-city split and rare-class reporting are also valuable evaluation choices.
weaknesses: Material concern: the central gait-compensation claim is not convincingly isolated or technically justified. GDC predicts only a global 2D translation from a single image, whereas gait-induced roll, pitch, parallax, and annular-camera distortion generally produce spatially varying motion. A sampling-coordinate translation also cannot undo within-exposure motion blur, despite the paper describing it as recovering sharper, less blur-contaminated features. Moreover, adding GDC simultaneously changes the lifting operation from integer gathering to bilinear sampling, so the small +0.39 mIoU gain cannot be attributed specifically to learned gait compensation. There is no comparison to measured IMU/camera motion or an ablation of bilinear sampling alone.

Material concern: QuadOcc ground-truth semantics are initialized by running Grounded-SAM on the same panoramic images used as model input and then transferring those labels to LiDAR. This creates correlated image-derived label noise and may favor vision methods that reproduce the initializer's biases. The manuscript gives no quantitative label-quality audit, manually annotated test subset, inter-annotator agreement, retained-voxel rate, or comparison against independently labeled 3D ground truth. Statements that the labels are robust and suitable for benchmarking therefore lack adequate evidence.

Material concern: the real-world evidence is narrow and statistically weak. QuadOcc contains only 10 campus scenes, reports validation rather than a held-out test set, and does not specify the exact train/validation scene allocation. Its main gain over MonoScene is only 1.37 mIoU, while individual module increments are 0.26–0.41 and no multi-seed variation or uncertainty is reported. H3O is entirely synthetic, uses one 12/4-map split, and therefore cannot establish the claimed robustness for real humanoid deployment.

The main ablation is cumulative rather than factorial: GDC, DP-ER, BGV, and AMoE-3D are added in a fixed order. It does not reveal independent effects or interactions, and it is unclear whether the Q0-to-full sequence also changes encoder/decoder capacity. The H3O experiments test selected components but do not provide a complete matched ablation of the full method. This is important because the dual-projection QuadOcc model has 189.83M parameters versus 148.9M for MonoScene, while its dual-projection gain over ER-only is only 0.53 mIoU.

Several analyses overstate what their protocols demonstrate. The field-of-view study crops a model trained at 360 degrees without retraining, confounding sensor coverage with distribution shift. The purported far-range result in Table 8 evaluates the full ±12.8 m footprint, including the near region, rather than a disjoint outer range. The calibration experiment models extrinsic error as per-point pixel offsets rather than physically valid SE(3) perturbations. These experiments do not cleanly support the associated claims about ring closure, far-field behavior, or calibration robustness.

Reproducibility and fairness are weakened by inconsistent spatial conventions. The datasets are described with z in [-2.0, 1.2] m, but several baseline configurations use origins implying [-1.2, 2.0] or [-2.4, 0.8]; OccRWKV is described with a forward-only x range [0, 25.6] despite the benchmark's symmetric range. Baselines also receive substantial method-specific changes, including altered positional encodings, widths, losses, heads, and proposal sources. Without released code and exact split files, it is difficult to establish voxel-level alignment or that the comparisons are controlled.

The claimed lightweight design needs qualification. The real QuadOcc configuration uses two encoders and 189.83M parameters, an 86.5% increase over its ER-only variant, for a 0.53 mIoU improvement. The main-paper efficiency numbers instead describe the 101.76M single-projection H3O configuration, which can leave an inaccurate impression of the deployed real-data model's cost. Presentation-only issues—including a Chinese label left in Figure 2, inconsistent terminology, and several equation/diagram inconsistencies—are secondary but further reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored setting: full-surround semantic scene completion from one panoramic camera on gait-driven robots. The combination of a real quadruped benchmark (QuadOcc) and a controlled synthetic human-ego benchmark (H3O) is a useful contribution to computer vision and embodied perception.

The empirical results are compelling, particularly on H3O: OneOcc improves over MonoScene from 33.46 to 37.29 mIoU within-city and from 24.15 to 32.23 mIoU cross-city. On QuadOcc it obtains the best camera-only semantic score (20.56 mIoU versus 19.19), including improvements on rare vehicles and pedestrians, although its geometric IoU remains below LMSCNet.

The evaluation is broader than the main tables alone suggest. The supplement examines field of view, Cartesian versus cylindrical grids, expert count and routing, calibration perturbations, temporal fusion, voxel resolution, distance ranges, lighting, parameters, memory, and measured Jetson AGX Orin latency. The cross-city split and adverse-condition analyses are especially valuable.

The component studies generally support the architecture: GDC, dual projection, bi-grid voxelization, and AMoE-3D raise QuadOcc mIoU successively from 19.19 to 19.58, 19.89, 20.30, and 20.56. Dedicated experiments also show that bi-grid processing improves both near- and far-range accuracy and that gradient-energy routing outperforms uniform routing.

The method is clearly motivated and mostly well presented, with useful equations, diagrams, baseline implementation details, dataset-construction descriptions, failure cases, and explicit discussion of resolution, sim-to-real, calibration, and temporal limitations. Embedded-device measurements provide stronger deployment evidence than desktop-GPU timing alone.
weaknesses: The claimed interpretation of GDC as gait-motion compensation is not cleanly established. It predicts only a global 2D translation from a single-frame feature map, without gait phase, IMU, exposure trajectory, or supervised displacement. Such a translation can absorb calibration or dataset biases rather than physical gait motion. More importantly, the GDC implementation simultaneously replaces MonoScene's integer lookup with bilinear sampling, so the reported +0.39 mIoU does not isolate learned compensation from the improved sampler. This is a material issue for one of the central claimed innovations.

QuadOcc ground-truth semantics are initialized by applying Grounded-SAM to the same panoramic imagery used as model input and transferring those labels to temporally aggregated LiDAR. Targeted manual correction is described, but no quantitative label audit, annotation agreement, retained-confidence rate, or comparison against independently annotated 3D labels is reported. Consequently, semantic evaluation may partly reward reproduction of the image teacher's biases, particularly for rare classes.

The real-data evidence is limited to ten campus scenes, and the manuscript does not precisely document the QuadOcc train/validation scene identities, counts, or separation beyond calling the split “sequence-heterogeneous.” Given 24K consecutive frames and stride-5 sampling, explicit proof that nearby frames or overlapping mapped regions cannot cross the split is important. The real-data advantage over MonoScene is also modest (1.37 mIoU), with no multi-seed variability or statistical uncertainty.

The lightweight characterization needs qualification. The full QuadOcc dual-projection model has 189.83M parameters, 26% more than MonoScene and 86.5% more than the ER-only OneOcc variant, for only +0.53 mIoU over ER-only. The main efficiency paragraph reports the 101.76M single-projection configuration without clearly distinguishing it from the full QuadOcc model, although the supplementary Jetson results do support favorable latency.

Several mechanistic conclusions are stronger than the experiments warrant. The main ablation is cumulative rather than factorial, so interactions and independent contributions are not established; the claimed cross-city robustness is evaluated only within synthetic CARLA data; and no real humanoid or cross-domain real-world transfer experiment is provided. These reservations limit the scope of the conclusions but do not outweigh the benchmark value and substantial H3O gains.

Some implementation notation remains ambiguous: the raw/equirectangular fusion operation is not fully specified in the lifting equations, and GradEnergy3D is written as a global squared norm even though subsequent 3D convolution and voxel-wise routing require a spatial energy map. Code and datasets are promised rather than available in the manuscript, making exact reproduction dependent on the eventual release.
